blocks.text: A number of devices operate by means of pressure difference that results from changes in the speed of the fluid.
1. Aeroplane Wings

The wing of an aeroplane is designed to deflect the air so that streamlines are closer together above the wing than below it as illustrated in Fig.5.17. We have seen that where the streamlines are forced closer together, the speed is faster. Thus, air is travelling faster on the upper side of the wing than on the lower. The pressure will be lower at the top of the wing, and the wing will be forced upward and the lift of an aeroplane is due to this effect.

blocks.alt: A side view of the rear of an aeroplane with a wing section in front of it. Green streamlines from the left crowd closely together over the curved upper surface of the wing and stay spread out below it, all moving to the right. Red arrows under the wing point upward.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.17: Lift of an aeroplane (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.17).

blocks.text: 2. Swing of a Ball

When a ball is thrown or kicked with spin, the ball is made smoother on one side by the bowler and remains rough on the other side. The air moves faster over rough side and slows over the smoother. According to Bernoulli's equation, the faster moving air creates lower pressure, while the slower moving air creates higher pressure, this pressure difference generates a sideways force, known as Magnus effect which causes the ball to curves in the air.

blocks.alt: A ball in an air stream that moves from right to left. Above the ball the streamlines crowd together (Faster air, lower pressure); below it they spread out (Slower air, higher pressure). An arrow labelled Deflection force points up from the ball. An inset labelled Spinning ball shows a small spinning ball whose path curves up away from a dashed straight line.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.18: Turbulent flow (air flow past a spinning ball) (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.18).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book captions this figure 'Turbulent flow', the caption of Fig. 5.13, but it shows air flowing past a spinning ball.
3. Filter Pump

A filter pump has a constriction in the centre, so that a jet of water from the tap flows faster here. This causes a drop in pressure near it and air, therefore, flows in from the side tube. The air and water together are expelled through the lower part of the pump.

blocks.alt: A filter pump in section. Water enters a tube at the top labelled Water and is forced through a narrow nozzle into a fast jet that runs down the body of the pump and leaves at the bottom outlet. A side tube on the right, labelled Air flow, has an arrow showing air flowing in towards the jet.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.19: Turbulent flow (filter pump) (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.19).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book also captions this figure (Fig. 5.19) ‘Turbulent flow’, but it shows a filter pump: a fast water jet at the constriction lowers the pressure and draws in air from the side tube.
4. Carburetor

The carburetor of a car engine uses a Venturi duct to feed the correct mixture of air and petrol to the cylinders. Air is drawn through the duct and along a pipe to the cylinders. A tiny inlet at the side of duct is fed with petrol.
The air through the duct moves very fast, creating low pressure in the duct, which draws petrol vapours into the air stream.

blocks.alt: A vertical Venturi duct with Air entering at the top. The duct narrows to a throat, where streamlines with downward arrows crowd together, and widens again below. The throat is labelled Low pressure. On the left, a chamber labelled Gas, at Atmospheric pressure, is joined to the throat by a bent pipe.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.20: Carburetor of an engine (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.20).

blocks.text: 5. Paint Sprayer

A stream of air passing over a tube dipped in a liquid will cause the liquid to rise in the tube as shown in Fig. 5.21. This effect is used in perfume bottles and paint sprayers. Actually when the rubber ball of atomizer is squeezed, the air is blown through tube and it rushes out through the narrow aperture with high speed and it causes fall of pressure. So, the atmospheric pressure pushes the perfume up leading to the narrow aperture.

blocks.alt: Air, shown by a blue arrow, enters a line that narrows to a nozzle on the right. A vertical tube dips from the nozzle into a container of red paint; red arrows show the paint rising up the tube and being sprayed out of the nozzle. Blue arrows press down on the paint surface inside the container. Labels: Air, Nozzle, Paint.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.21: A stream of air passing over a tube dipped in a liquid (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.21).

blocks.text: 6. Venturi Relation
Consider a pipe within which a fluid of density ρ is flowing through different areas of cross-section as shown in the Fig. 5.22.
Let A₁ be the cross-sectional area at wide end and A₂ be the cross-sectional area at narrow portion.
Suppose that v₁ and v₂ be the flow speeds at the wide and narrow portions respectively. Pressure P₁ and P₂ indicate the liquid pressure at both the portions by connecting the limbs of the manometer.

Three streamlines squeeze together through the throat; v1 is marked in the wide part and v2 in the throat. A U-tube manometer below joins the wide part and the throat: the level under the wide part, P1, is lower, and the level under the throat, P2, is higher by h.

7. Torricelli's Theorem

A simple application of Bernoulli's equation is shown in Fig. 5.23. Suppose a large tank of fluid has two small orifices A and B on it, as shown in Fig. 5.23. Let us find the speed with which the water flows from the orifice A.

blocks.alt: A tall tank of water whose surface, moving down with speed v1, is at height h1 above the bottom. Orifice A on the right, at height h2 above the bottom and h1 - h2 below the surface, lets out a jet with speed v2 that curves down. Orifice B, low on the left, leads into a tube that turns the jet upward (speed v3), and the water rises to the level of the water in the tank.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.23: A tank containing fluid with a orifice (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.23).

blocks.text: Since the orifices are so small, the efflux speeds v₂ and v₃ will be much larger than the speed v₁ of the top surface of water. We can therefore, take v₁ as approximately zero. Hence, Bernoulli's equation can be written as:

blocks.latex: P_1 + \rho g h_1 = P_2 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_2^2 + \rho g h_2

blocks.text: Therefore, the above equation becomes:
This is Torricelli's theorem which states that:

blocks.title: Torricelli's theorem
blocks.text: The speed of efflux is equal to the velocity gained by the fluid in falling through the distance (h₁ - h₂) under the action of gravity.

Notice that the speed of the efflux of liquid is the same as the speed of a ball that falls through a height (h₁ - h₂). The top level of the tank has moved down a little and the P.E. has been transferred into K.E. of the efflux of fluid. If the orifice had been pointed upward at B as shown in Fig.6.4, this K.E. would allow the liquid to rise to the level of water tank. In practice, viscous-energy losses would alter the result to some extent.
